topic.name: Surface Areas of Revolution for Parametric Curves

question.text: Consider the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = 2e^t, \quad y = 2e^{-t}, \quad t\in \left[-2,2\right]. \] What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s. \]

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=-2$ to $t_2=2.$

Computing the derivatives, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} ( 2e^t ) = 2e^t\\[5pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} ( 2e^{-t} ) = -2e^{-t}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{-2}^{2} 2e^{t} \sqrt{\left(2e^t\right)^2+\left(-2e^{-t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \sqrt{4e^{2t}+ 4e^{-2t}}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \sqrt{4(e^{2t}+ e^{-2t})}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t}\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{(e^{2t}+ e^{-2t})}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 8\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \sqrt{e^{2t}+ e^{-2t}}\,\textrm d t. \end{align*}

Now, using the definition of the hyperbolic cosine $\cosh 2t =\dfrac{e^{2t}+ e^{-2t}}{2},$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

\begin{align*} S &= 8\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \sqrt{e^{2t}+ e^{-2t}}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= 8\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \sqrt{2\cosh 2t}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 8\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \cdot\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{\cosh 2t}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 8\sqrt{2}\pi \int_{-2}^{2} e^{t} \sqrt{\cosh 2t}\,\textrm d t. \end{align*}

example.title: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y

question.text: Consider the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = 2e^{t/2}, \quad y =e^{t}, \quad t\in \left[0,\ln{3}\right]. \] Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis.
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s. \]

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\ln{3}.$

Computing the derivatives, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} ( 2e^{t/2} ) = e^{t/2}\\[5pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} (e^{t} ) = e^{t}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{\ln{3}} 2e^{t/2} \sqrt{\left(e^{t/2}\right)^2+\left(e^{t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{\ln{3}}2e^{t/2} \sqrt{e^{t} + e^{2t}}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{\ln{3}}2e^{t/2} \sqrt{e^{t}(1+e^{t})}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=4\pi \int_{0}^{\ln{3}}e^{t/2}\cdot e^{t/2}\sqrt{1+e^{t}}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{0}^{\ln{3}} e^{t} \sqrt{1+e^{t}}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] \end{align*}

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+e^{t}.$ Then, $\textrm{d}u = e^{t} \,\textrm d t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.

$t$ $0$ $\ln{3}$
$u$ $2$ $4$

Therefore, we get

\begin{align*} S &=4\pi \int_{0}^{\ln{3}} e^{t} \sqrt{1+e^{t}}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{2}^{4} \sqrt{u} \,\textrm d u \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \int_{2}^{4} u^{1/2} \,\textrm d u \\[5pt] &= 4\pi\cdot \left.\dfrac{2u^{3/2}}{3}\right|_2^4 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8\pi}{3}\left(4^{3/2} - 2^{3/2}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8\pi}{3}(8-2\sqrt{2}) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}(4-\sqrt{2}). \end{align*}

example.title: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution

question.text: Consider the curve defined parametrically as \[ x = t^3, \quad y = 2t, \quad t\in \left[0,2\right]. \] What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s. \]

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=2.$

Computing the derivatives, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} ( t^3 ) = 3t^2\\[5pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} ( 2t ) =2. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{2} t^3 \sqrt{\left(3t^2\right)^2+\left(2\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{2} t^3 \sqrt{9t^4+4}\,\textrm d t. \end{align*}

example.title: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y

question.text:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 
\[
x = t^2, \quad y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}t^{4}, \quad t \in \left[0,\sqrt[4]{6}\right].
\]
Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula \[ S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s. \]

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have \[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

Therefore, we will use \[ S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\sqrt[4]{6}.$

Computing the derivatives, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t} \left(t^2\right) = 2t,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}t^{4}\right) = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}t^3. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} S &=2\pi \int_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}} t^2\sqrt{(2t)^2+\left(\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}t^3\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}} t^2\sqrt{4t^2+\dfrac{16}{3}t^6}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}} t^2\sqrt{4t^2\left(1+\dfrac{4}{3}t^4\right)}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}} t^2\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4}{3}t^4}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &=4\pi \int_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}} \sqrt{1+\dfrac{4}{3}t^4}\cdot t^{3}\,\textrm d t. \end{align*}

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+\dfrac{4}{3}t^{4}.$ Then, $\textrm{d}u = \dfrac{16}{3}t^3 \,\textrm d t \Longrightarrow t^3\,\textrm d t = \dfrac{3}{16}\textrm d u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u{:}$

$t$ $0$ $\sqrt[4]{6}$
$u$ $1$ $9$

Therefore, we get \begin{align*} S &=4\pi \int_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}} \sqrt{1+\dfrac{4}{3}t^4}\cdot t^{3}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=4\pi \int_{1}^{9} \sqrt{u}\cdot \dfrac{3}{16}\,\textrm d u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\int_{1}^{9} u^{1/2}\,\textrm d u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\cdot \left[\dfrac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{1}^{9}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}\right]\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left(27-1\right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{13\pi}. \end{align*}

example.title: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution

question.text:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 
\[
x = \cos t + \ln\left(\tan\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\right), \quad y = \sin t, \quad t \in \left[\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right].
\]
Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula \[ S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s. \]

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have \[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

Therefore, we will use \[ S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=\frac{\pi}{3}$ to $t_2=\frac{\pi}{2}.$

Computing the derivatives, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} &=\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}\left(\cos t + \ln\left(\tan\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\right)\right) \\[5pt] &=-\sin t + \dfrac{1}{\tan(t/2)}\cdot \sec^2\left(\frac{t}{2}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &=-\sin t + \csc t,\\[10pt] \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} &=\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}\left(\sin t\right) \\[5pt] &=\cos t. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} S &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sin t \sqrt{\left(\csc t - \sin t\right)^2+\left(\cos t\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sin t \sqrt{\csc^2 t - 2 + \sin^2 t + \cos^2 t}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sin t \sqrt{\csc^2 t - 2 + 1}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sin t \sqrt{\csc^2 t - 1}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sin t \sqrt{\cot^2 t}\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sin t \cot t\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &=2\pi \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \cos t\,\textrm d t. \end{align*}

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = \sin t.$ Then, $\textrm{d}u = \cos t \,\textrm d t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u{:}$

$t$ $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
$u$ $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $1$

Therefore, we get \begin{align*} S &=\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} 2\pi \cos t\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &=\int_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} 2\pi \,\textrm d u\\[5pt] &=2\pi \left[u\right]_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}\\[5pt] &=2\pi \left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\pi(2 - \sqrt{3})}. \end{align*}
